column2: follow-up question (asked when this keyPoint is uncertain; must not contain the answer)
When milk is left out in summer and turns sour, what has happened to the original substance, and what does that tell you about the kind of change?
If you watched a test tube where two clear liquids were mixed, what are the things you could look for to decide whether something new had formed?
Burning magnesium in oxygen takes a whole sentence to describe. What is the shortest simple way to write it, and which substances go in which place?
In a written reaction, how do you show which substances are used up, which are formed, and which way the change goes?
If you swap the names in a reaction for symbols, what do you gain, and what do we call it when the atom counts do not yet match?
A burning log leaves a small pile of ash. Why can a reaction's atoms not simply vanish, and what must we therefore do to a written reaction?
How would you check whether the number of atoms of each element matches on the two sides of an arrow?
When you try to balance a reaction, which part of a formula are you allowed to change, which part must you leave alone, and where is it sensible to begin?
A balanced equation does not say whether iron is a solid or water is steam. What small marks can be added to the formulae to show this?
Some reactions only happen when heated or with a helper substance. Where in a written reaction can that information be placed?
When quick lime is dropped into water, what happens to the beaker, and what single new substance forms?
What is special about the number of products compared with the number of starting substances in this kind of reaction?
Why does a whitewashed wall look dull at first and then shiny after a few days?
If a reaction makes its surroundings warm, what do we call it, and what is being given out?
How can the food we eat give us warmth, and what do we call the process in our cells that does this?
Some reactions make a test tube feel cold when you touch it. What is happening to energy in them?
When a green crystal is heated and breaks down into simpler substances, how is the number of starting substances different from the number of products?
What do we call a breakdown that is caused by heating, and what two products form when the common calcium-containing rock used in building is heated?
When current is passed through acidified water, what do you see at the two metal rods dipped in it, and are the amounts of gas collected the same?
Why does a white silver salt used in old photography slowly turn grey when left in sunlight, and what two things are formed?
When a clean iron nail sits in blue copper sulphate solution, what happens to the nail and the solution, and what has swapped places?
Why can zinc or lead take the place of copper in a copper compound, but not the other way round?
If two clear solutions are mixed and a white solid appears, what is that solid called and what kind of reaction is this?
In the reaction of sodium sulphate with barium chloride, what exactly passes between the two reacting solutions?
When a substance takes up oxygen, what is that process called, and what is the name for the opposite change where it gives up oxygen?
When hydrogen is passed over hot black copper oxide, which substance is oxidised and which is reduced, and why are such reactions grouped together?
What do we call the slow damage of a metal's surface by the things around it, such as damp air?
What colours do iron, silver and copper develop when they are left exposed, and what is that on iron commonly called?
What happens to the smell and taste of fats and oils when they are left for a long time, and why?
Name some ways in which food makers stop packaged chips and oily food from spoiling.
How would you tell, without tasting, which of two solutions is an acid and which is a base, using the two colours of a natural dye paper?
Why does a yellow stain from a spicy dish change colour when scrubbed with a cleaning bar, and what brings the original colour back?
Besides colour changes, what other change in a substance can show whether a solution is acidic or basic?
When a piece of zinc is dropped into a dilute acid, what do you see, and what does the metal do to the acid?
If a metal is warmed with a strong alkali solution, can it also give off a gas? Is that true for every metal?
When the gas released by a carbonate and an acid is bubbled through calcium hydroxide solution, what do you observe, and which gas is it?
What three things form whenever a carbonate or a hydrogencarbonate meets an acid, and which everyday rocks are made of calcium carbonate?
When black copper oxide is stirred into dilute hydrochloric acid, what colour does the solution turn, and what has made that colour?
What kind of oxides do metals form, judging from what they give on reacting with an acid, and what are the products?
The gas formed when a non-metal like carbon burns reacts with a base, as it did with lime water. What does this suggest about the nature of the oxides of non-metals?
What is the name for the reaction in which sodium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid cancel each other's effects, and what do they form together?
Alcohol and glucose both contain hydrogen but are not acids. What does this tell us about hydrogen alone?
In the bulb-and-nails set-up, what makes the bulb glow with acid but not with glucose?
Which kind of particle in a solution makes it acidic, and which makes it basic?
Why does dry hydrogen chloride gas leave dry litmus paper unchanged, but the gas dissolved in water turns it red?
What do bases give in water, and what is the special name for a base that dissolves in water?
When concentrated sulphuric acid is dripped into water, what does the beaker feel like, and what does this tell you about the process?
Why must an acid always be poured into water instead of water into the acid, and what could go wrong otherwise?
What happens to the number of ions in each unit of volume when more water is mixed in, and what is this process called?
How can one special indicator paper that gives many colours help you find how acidic or basic a solution is?
What is the scale used to express hydrogen ion concentration called, what are its two ends, and what does the letter p stand for?
If one solution has more hydronium ions than another, which one has the lower number on the scale, and what number marks a neutral solution?
Two acids are made up to equal strength of solution but give unequal numbers of hydrogen ions. What does the strength of an acid depend on?
How do we describe an acid that gives many hydrogen ions compared with one that gives few?
Within what narrow range does the body work, and what does that mean for how much change living things can tolerate?
What happens to rivers and the life in them when rain water becomes unusually acidic?
Why does an upset stomach feel better after taking a mild base such as milk of magnesia?
What lowers the acidity of the mouth after a sweet snack, and what part of the tooth is damaged by it?
What kind of substance is left by a honey-bee sting, and what does the hair of a stinging wild plant inject?
What can you rub on a bee sting for relief, and what grows beside nettle that helps?
How do chemists put salts that share a metal or a non-metal part into the same group, and can you give a pair from the sodium group?
How does the strength of the acid and of the base that a salt is made from decide the pH of that salt?
What happens to concentrated salt solution in a cell with two electrodes carrying current, and what is this industrial process named after?
At which electrode does each gas appear in that process, and where does the alkali form?
What gas from the electrolysis of brine is used to make bleaching powder, and what does it act upon?
Name some uses of this white powder in making cloth and paper white, in industry, and in making water safe to drink.
What is the chemical name of the compound used in the kitchen to make pakoras crisp, and what makes it a mild base?
Why does a cake rise and become light when a certain raising agent is used, and which gas is responsible?
How is the hydrated cleaning salt obtained starting from the kitchen powder, and what kind of salt is it?
Which industries and household jobs use this cleaning salt, and what does it do to hard water?
Blue crystals that look dry turn white on heating and blue again on moistening. What does this show they contain?
What does the term water of crystallisation mean, and how many molecules of it does copper sulphate hold?
What substance is obtained on heating the hydrated calcium sulphate salt at a moderate temperature, and what is it commonly called?
What happens when this material meets water, and why do doctors use it to support broken bones?
What do we call the property of metals that lets them be hammered into thin sheets, and which metals show it most?
What do we call the ability of metals to be drawn into wires, and which metal is the best example?
Which metals are the best conductors of heat, which are poor, and why are such metals used for cooking vessels?
Why are the metal cables that carry current at home covered with a plastic coat, and what property of the metal makes them useful?
What do we call metals that make a ringing sound when struck on a hard surface, and where is this used?
Which non-metal is a liquid at room temperature, and what states are the others in?
How do non-metals compare with metals in shaping and in conducting heat and electricity, and which one is a notable exception?
Which metal is a liquid at room temperature, and which other two metals will melt if held in your hand?
A hard gemstone and the soft black material in pencils are both made only of carbon. How do their hardness and electrical conduction differ, and what are such different forms of one element called?
What forms when a metal is heated in air, and what colour is it for copper?
Why must sodium and potassium be stored under a liquid, and what would happen otherwise?
Why does an aluminium utensil stay unchanged for years even though aluminium is quite reactive?
What name is given to oxides that react with both acids and bases, and which two metals give examples?
Which metal oxides dissolve in water, and what do they form?
What are the products when a metal reacts with water, and what further happens to an oxide that dissolves?
What happens when sodium or potassium is put into cold water, and why does the gas burn?
Why does a reactive metal that reacts gently with water start floating, and what does the next metal below it need in order to react with water?
Which metals need steam to react, and which metals show no reaction with water whatsoever?
In the test with dilute hydrochloric acid, which metal gave the quickest bubbling, what was the order of the others, and what happened with copper?
Why does a strong oxidising acid not release hydrogen with metals, and which two metals are exceptions?
What is aqua regia, which two acids make it, and in what proportion are they mixed?
What can this mixture dissolve that neither acid can on its own, and how would you describe the liquid?
If one metal pushes another metal out of the solution of its salt, which of the two is the more reactive?
Which metal sits at the top of the list of metals in decreasing order of activity, which at the bottom, and where is hydrogen placed?
Why do the elements of group 18 show hardly any chemical activity, and what do other elements try to do?
What happens to a sodium atom's outer electron when it reacts, and what charge does it end up with?
What happens to chlorine in the same reaction, and what charge does it end up with?
What do we call compounds formed when electrons pass from a metal to a non-metal?
What holds the ions of table salt together, and is salt made of separate molecules?
Why do solids made of ions need a lot of heat before they melt or boil?
In which states do these compounds carry current, and why not as a solid?
What do we call a naturally occurring element or compound in the earth's crust, and what is it called when the metal can be profitably taken from it?
Which metals are found free, which are never found free, and in what forms do the middle ones occur?
What is the name for the soil and sand mixed in a mined ore, and why must it be taken out before extracting the metal?
Why do the oxides of metals near the bottom of the reactivity list change into the metals on heating alone?
How is the liquid metal obtained from its red ore when it is heated in air?
What is the difference between roasting and calcination in terms of the kind of ore and the amount of air supplied?
After an ore is turned into an oxide, how is the metal then obtained, with an example?
Why can aluminium be used instead of carbon to free some metals from their oxides?
Why is the reaction used to join broken railway lines so hot, and what is it called?
Why can carbon not free the metals at the top of the list from their oxides?
At which electrodes do the metal and chlorine appear when a molten chloride is electrolysed?
In refining copper by electricity, which block is the impure metal, which is the thin pure strip, and what liquid is used?
Where does the pure metal go during the process, and what happens to the impurities?
Why does silver turn black and copper turn green when left in the open?
What is the brown flaky coating on iron called, and what is the general process of metals being attacked called?
In the three-test-tube experiment, in which tube did the nails go brown, and what does it tell you about what iron needs?
Name some ways of keeping an iron object from going brown and flaky.
Why does a coated iron bucket stay safe even after the coating is scratched?
Why is pure iron hardly ever used, and what do small additions do to it?
What do we call a uniform blend of metals with each other or with a non-metal, and how is one prepared?
Compared with salts, how do the melting points and conduction of carbon compounds look, and what does that say about ions?
Why does an atom with four outer electrons not simply give them up or take four more?
What does carbon do instead, and what does each atom end up with?
How is a bond formed when two hydrogen atoms come together?
How many pairs of electrons are shared between two oxygen atoms and between two nitrogen atoms, and what are those bonds called?
Why are molecules with strong inner bonds still easy to melt, and why do they conduct poorly?
Diamond and graphite are both made of the same atoms. What makes them so different?
How is each carbon atom connected in diamond and how in graphite?
How do hardness and electrical conduction compare in the two, and do their chemical properties differ?
What is the name for carbon atoms linking to one another to build big molecules in straight, branched or closed shapes?
Why do other elements fail to match carbon's ability to link up with itself, even the one that comes closest below it in the periodic table?
How many other atoms can one carbon atom bond to, and with which other elements?
How does the size of a carbon atom affect how tightly it holds shared electrons, and why does that make its compounds stable?
Carbon compounds in which all links between carbon atoms are single bonds are what kind, and how reactive are they?
If a compound has a double or triple bond between carbons, what kind is it and how reactive is it compared with the other?
Besides straight chains, what other shapes can carbon skeletons take, and can each of these have single bonds only or also double bonds?
What name is given to compounds built from just these two elements, and how are the three families of them distinguished?
Two molecules have the same formula but different shapes. What are they called?
What do you call an atom that takes the place of hydrogen in a carbon chain, such as oxygen or a halogen?
Why do some groups of atoms decide a compound's properties whatever the length of the carbon chain?
What do you call a series of compounds with the same group on chains of different lengths, such as the four simplest alcohols?
As the chain gets longer along the series, which properties change gradually and which stay similar?
How do you choose the root of a compound's name from its carbon count, and what two kinds of additions can show the attached group?
How are the names for the ketone with three carbons and for the alkene with three carbons built?
What does carbon give when it burns in air, and what else is released?
How do flames of saturated and unsaturated compounds differ, and what happens when the air supply is limited?
If the bottom of a cooking vessel turns black, what does that tell you about the stove?
Besides burning, what other change can turn an alcohol into something acidic?
What do you call a substance that adds oxygen, and name two used to turn alcohols into acids.
What does an unsaturated compound take up with a nickel or palladium helper, and what helps the helper stay unchanged?
How is a liquid vegetable oil turned into a solid fat, and how do the carbon chains of oils compare with those of fats from animals?
Why does a saturated hydrocarbon normally not react with common chemicals, and what is needed for chlorine to react with it quickly?
Why is the reaction of methane with chlorine in sunlight called a swapping reaction?
Is ethanol a solid, liquid or gas at room temperature, and what is it used for in medicine?
What can even a small amount of the pure form do to a person, and why is that dangerous for health?
Why is alcohol meant for industry made undrinkable and coloured?
What gas is given off when sodium is added to ethanol, and what other product forms?
What does strong heating of ethanol with the very concentrated acid used in labs produce, and what role does the acid play?
What is the other name of ethanoic acid, and what is a dilute water solution of it used for?
Why does pure ethanoic acid sometimes turn into ice in winter, and what name did that give it?
How does ethanoic acid compare with hydrochloric acid in how fully it breaks into ions?
What forms when an acid and an alcohol are warmed together with a few drops of a strong acid?
What happens when this product is treated with an alkali, and why is the reaction named after soap?
What gas is formed when the weak organic acid meets baking soda, and how can you show it?
Why does oily dirt not wash off with water alone, and which end of a soap molecule faces which?
In a cluster of soap molecules around dirt, which end faces inwards and which outwards, and what does the cluster do to the dirt?
Why does soap form a sticky solid and little foam in hard water?
Why can cleaners that are not soaps still work in hard water?
A plant that seems not to grow at all is still alive. What does that show about using movement alone to define life?
Why must living things keep working on their structures even when they are not doing anything?
What do we call the processes that must continue even during sleep, and why do they need energy?
Name the four kinds of process an organism needs for taking in materials, getting energy, moving things around the body and removing wastes.
Why does an Amoeba not need special organs for taking in food and gases?
Why can simple spreading out not serve all the cells of a large body?
What do we call organisms that make their own food from simple inorganic raw materials, and what are some examples?
Which organisms depend on the first group for their food, and what helps them break their food down?
What does a green plant convert, using light and a green pigment, and into what?
Where does a plant keep the carbohydrate it does not use immediately, and what do we store in our own bodies?
What are the small green structures seen in leaf cells, and what did the leaf with pale patches show?
What are the three events that take place in making food, starting with absorbing light?
How can a plant in the desert separate these steps in time?
What are the very small openings on a leaf's surface for, and why does the plant shut them at times?
What makes a pore open and what makes it close?
From where does a land plant get its water and minerals, and in what forms does it take nitrogen?
How do mushrooms and moulds get their food compared with organisms that swallow it whole?
What do we call organisms that live on a host without killing it, and name a few?
How does an Amoeba catch a food particle, and what is formed around it?
What happens inside that structure, and how is leftover material dealt with?
Which gland's fluid has an enzyme in it, which food does it act on, and what is formed?
How is food pushed along the long tube, and what is that movement called?
Which glands in the stomach wall release acid, a protein-digesting enzyme and a slimy fluid?
What does the acid do for the enzyme, and what protects the stomach from the acid?
Why must the food coming from the stomach be treated before the gland's enzymes can act, and what breaks big fat drops into smaller ones?
Which enzymes does the gland below the stomach provide, and what are the final products of digestion?
What finger-like structures line the small intestine, and how do they help absorb food?
Why does a cow's gut need to be longer than a tiger's for digesting its meal?
Into what molecule is the six-carbon sugar first broken, and in which part of the cell does this happen?
What are the products when this molecule is broken down in yeast without air, and what is the process called?
Where does the breakdown with oxygen take place, and what are its products?
What happens in a tired muscle that has too little oxygen, and what effect does it have?
What molecule is made from the energy released in respiration, and what is it called?
How does this molecule supply energy to the cell, and name some things it powers.
When do plants release carbon dioxide and when do they release oxygen, and how do the gases move in and out?
Why do fish breathe much faster than land animals?
How is the air cleaned on its way to the chest, and what keeps the windpipe open?
What are the tiny air sacs at the end of the lung passages where gases are exchanged, and what do their walls contain?
What happens to the ribs and the muscle below the lungs when we breathe in, and how do gases pass between air and blood?
Why does a large animal need something in its blood to carry oxygen, rather than relying on spreading out?
What carries oxygen in human blood, where is it found, and how strongly does it hold the gas?
Is carbon dioxide carried the same way as oxygen? What helps it travel?
What is the watery part of blood called, and what does it carry compared with the red cells?
What three parts must a transport system have for blood to reach every tissue?
Why is the heart divided into chambers, and which side handles blood from the lungs?
Why is separating the two kinds of blood so important for animals that keep a steady body temperature?
How many chambers do the hearts of fishes and of mammals have, and how often does blood pass through the heart in one full cycle in each?
Why do the vessels that take blood from the heart have thick, stretchy walls?
How do the vessels that bring blood back to the heart prevent it flowing the wrong way?
In which tiny vessels does exchange between blood and cells take place, and why there?
What stops bleeding after an injury, and why does it matter for the pressure of the system?
What is the fluid that leaks from capillaries into spaces between cells called, and how does it differ from blood plasma in colour and protein content?
Why does a tall plant, where the parts making food are far from the parts taking up materials, need a transport system?
Which tube carries water and minerals, and which carries the food made in the leaves?
How does water get into the root and begin to climb the xylem, and why is that push by itself insufficient for a tall tree?
What pulls water up from the roots when water evaporates from the leaves, and what is that loss called?
Which driving force matters at night and which in daytime?
What is the movement of soluble food in a plant called, and which tissue carries it?
Why does this movement need energy, and what supplies it?
What do we call the removal of harmful nitrogen-containing wastes from the body?
What are the main organs that make and pass out urine, in order?
What does the filtering unit of the kidney consist of?
Which useful substances are taken back as the filtrate moves along the tube, and what decides how much water is taken back?
Why can people with failed kidneys need a machine, and what does it remove?
How does the cleaning fluid in the machine differ from blood, and how do the wastes move?
Where do plants keep waste products, and what happens to some of them in leaves?
